### Show the distributions of values visually. Explain, in comments, what those distributions mean statistically. Be thorough.
```{r}
# path is hard coded to dataset, can easily replace with your path
data <- read.csv(
  "C:\\Users\\Gabe\\Documents\\GitHub\\data_science_classes_windows\\data\\sales_data_sample.csv"
)


# display the first 6 rows of the data
head(data)

# print each column with its type - str is structure of data
str(data)


# aes() - Aesthetic mapping. It defines how data variables are represented visually in the plot.
# For example, mapping X to dates and Y to sales values.

# Another use of aes() is mapping y to ..density.., which shows the density of the data
# rather than the raw counts in the histogram.

# Density is calculated as a normalized value, not simply the proportion of a bin's count.
# The formula for density is:

# Density = Count of items in bin / (Bin width * Total number of items)

# Sets TotalSales as the variable on the X-axis.

# geom_histogram() uses aes() to map data variables to the visual components of the histogram.

# ! Remember, ggplot takes the first arg as data, then we reference individual columns, similar to data$Column


# Get the number of rows
number_of_rows <- nrow(data)
sqrt_number_of_rows <- round(sqrt(number_of_rows))
# This is used for binning
sqrt_number_of_rows

# Add layers using the + operator
# Histogram uses density on the y-axis and bins on the x-axis
# A good rule for the number of bins is the square root of the number of data points
# The density curve adds a smooth outline of the distribution
# 'alpha' controls the transparency of the density fill

ggplot(data, aes(x = TotalSales)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = ..density..),
    bins = sqrt_number_of_rows,
    fill = "skyblue", color = "black"
  ) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.3, fill = "red") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Sales (sqrt Density)", x = "Sales", y = "Density")

# Again, the y-axis should display Density = Count of items in bin / (Bin width * Total number of items)
```

Experiment with histogram binning for the categorical data in R. This is open-ended intentionally because this dataset isn’t ideal for binning, but I want you to build something using binning just to see how it works.

```{r}
# Binning is the process of grouping continuous data into discrete intervals, or "bins."
# For example, if values range from 0 to 100, counting each individual value may not be useful.
# Instead, binning groups similar values into categories to better understand the distribution.
#
# We can experiment with different numbers of bins—such as 5, 10, 20, or 30—to see how it affects the shape
# of the distribution. Does increasing or decreasing the number of bins reveal new patterns or obscure important details?
# Understanding this can help in choosing the most effective binning strategy for analysis and visualization.

# Previovusly we used the sqrt() for bins, but we can adjust half and twice the sqrt to see how the distriubtion changes
half_Sqrt <- round(sqrt_number_of_rows / 2)
twice_Sqrt <- sqrt_number_of_rows * 2

ggplot(data, aes(x = TotalSales)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = ..density..),
    bins = half_Sqrt,
    fill = "skyblue",
    color = "black"
  ) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.3, fill = "red") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Sales (sqrt Density /2)", x = "Sales", y = "Density")


ggplot(data, aes(x = TotalSales)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = ..density..),
    bins = twice_Sqrt,
    fill = "skyblue",
    color = "black"
  ) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.3, fill = "red") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Sales (sqrt Density x2)", x = "Sales", y = "Density")

print("Compared to the original distribution, halving the bins leads to a more nuanced distriubtion. The density line is less bumpy and erratic. By comparison, the larger number of bins. The sqrt /2 density also had the geom density curve bending above the bars whereas the 2x density kept the curve below the bars.")
```

Show the values of central tendency, both numerically and visually. Interpret those values in your own words in Markdown.

```{r}
# Measures of Central Tendency:
# - Mean: The average of all values.
# - Median: The middle value when the data is sorted.
# - Mode: The most frequently occurring value.

# Calculate statistics
Mean <- mean(data$TotalSales, na.rm = TRUE)
Median <- median(data$TotalSales, na.rm = TRUE)
Mode <- as.numeric(names(which.max(table(data$TotalSales)))) # Ensure numeric, but this was sufficient as a string

# Print results
cat("Mean is:", Mean, "\nMedian is:", Median, "\nMode is:", Mode, "\n")

# ! Data shows the
ggplot(data, aes(x = TotalSales)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10, fill = "skyblue") +
  geom_vline(
    aes(
      xintercept = Mean,
      color = "Mean",
      linetype = "Mean"
    ),
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    aes(
      xintercept = Median,
      color = "Median",
      linetype = "Median"
    ),
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    name = "Central Tendencies",
    values = c("Mean" = "red", "Median" = "black")
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c("Mean" = "solid", "Median" = "solid"),
    guide = "none"
  )
labs(title = "Total Sales Distribution", x = "Total Sales", y = "Frequency")

print(
  "As we can see, the mode is displayed with the largest bar (22). This histogram shows the mean and median."
)
```

Visually depict the Interquartile range. Interpret the IQR for the dataset (in Markdown).

```{r}
# Boxplot for TotalSales
boxplot(
  data$TotalSales,
  main = "Boxplot of Total Sales",
  ylab = "Total Sales",
  col = "lightblue",
  border = "darkblue"
)

# Calculate IQR using native IQR function. As a reminder, IQR simply means how wide the 50% of your data is. Box charts are BEST for they display the IQR. As a bonus, we also get to see the mean again.
iqr_value <- IQR(data$TotalSales)
iqr_value
```

Create the statistics moments for the dataset.

```{r}
# Statistical moments are numerical values that describe the shape and characteristics of a distribution.
# While the concept may be less familiar outside of statistics, they're quite intuitive:
#
# - Mean: The average of the values (1st moment)
# - Variance: The spread of the data around the mean (2nd moment)
# - Skewness: The asymmetry of the distribution (3rd moment)
# - Kurtosis: The "fatness" of the tails — tells us whether the distribution has heavier or lighter tails
#             compared to a normal (Gaussian) distribution. This is often easier to interpret visually using line charts.

variance <- var(data$TotalSales)
skewness <- skewness(data$TotalSales)
kurtosis_val <- kurtosis(data$TotalSales)

cat("Mean is still :", Mean, "\nVariance is:", variance, "\nSkewness is:", skewness, "\nKurtosis is:", kurtosis_val)
# Also....I just found out you can get all of these from a library called psych


description <- describe(data$TotalSales)
# note, psych library gives us excess kurtosis whereas moments gives us regular kurtosis. Moments typically refers to the regular.
description
```
